newsitem.title: UK: Sterling clambers to new 59-month highs vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Sterling clambers to new 59-month highs vs mark.

text.p: Sterling clambered above 2.88 marks on Tuesday for the first time in almost five years, building on the two percent rally it has staged in the past week amid expectations of higher UK interest rates.

A slew of stronger-than-expected economic reports last week and a survey by the Royal Institute of Chartered Surveyors released on Tuesday indicated that consumption and the property market remain buoyant despite the two quarter-percentage point rate rises seen since Labour came to power in May.
This has fanned hopes the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee will raise rates from 6.5 percent next month.
Traders have also been revising up how far rates need to rise to keep inflation in check, adding fuel to sterling's rally.

"Sterling is being driven by concern that interest rates will get jacked up sharply," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "It's going to hit a ceiling at some point, but it will be hard to call that point until sentiment changes."

The pound rose to 2.8818 marks, its best showing since July 1992. It was at 2.8775/85 marks at 1000 GMT versus 2.8725/35 late Monday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6682/88 compared to the five-month high of $1.6725 it set yesterday and $1.6682/92 in Europe late on Monday.
Sterling's trade-weighted index, which has surged more than 20 percent since August 1996, was at 101.9 versus 101.5 Monday.

These gains have eroded UK exporters' competitiveness and the value of their foreign-currency earnings. Shares in British Steel and Imperial Chemical Industries slumped on Monday amid concern about the impact of sterling strength.

"Markets tend to overshoot, so we could see sterling/mark at 2.95 marks and get people talking about three," said Warwick Lightfoot, treasury economist at Royal Bank of Scotland. "But there is an element of doubt whether this will last given that the pound is definitely overvalued at these levels."
Signs that the government is becoming more sympathetic to the UK exporters' plight could trigger a pullback in the pound.
"Brown has already said that he favours a competitive pound," said Coleman at CIBC Wood Gundy. "If he repeats that, it would catch people's attention."

Traders are also looking for direction to the budget Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown is due to present on July 2. A net fiscal tightening of three to four billion pounds will help rein in consumption and could reduce the need for rates to rise as quickly as traders are currently discounting.

September short sterling is at 92.95 percent, giving an implied yield of 7.05 percent. This indicates the market is looking for rates to rise by half a percentage point by the end of the third quarter.
